draft.body:
# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

live_draft_blocks.content: I started this inquiry at the east gate, unsure whether to wait for the shuttle or walk. The pilot data show 160 boardings in week A and 240 in week B [@lyra:1]. These totals track trips, not unique people, and the two weeks differed in academic schedule [@lyra:1]. Because the pilot was not randomized and no attendance data were collected [@lyra:1], the increase in boardings cannot be attributed to the shuttle changing class attendance. The evidence supports further investigation into usage patterns, not a causal link to academic presence. I want this paragraph to keep my uncertainty visible rather than sound more certain than the evidence allows.

blocks.content: I started this inquiry at the east gate, unsure whether to wait for the shuttle or walk. The pilot data show 160 boardings in week A and 240 in week B [@lyra:1]. These totals track trips, not unique people, and the two weeks differed in academic schedule [@lyra:1]. Because the pilot was not randomized and no attendance data were collected [@lyra:1], the increase in boardings cannot be attributed to the shuttle changing class attendance. The evidence supports further investigation into usage patterns, not a causal link to academic presence. I want this paragraph to keep my uncertainty visible rather than sound more certain than the evidence allows.

blocks.heading: Evidence
blocks.content: The rider survey compounds this ambiguity by measuring only a subset of the population. Eighteen voluntary responses came from people already using the shuttle, and fourteen of them valued the later service [@lyra:2]. However, non-riders were not surveyed [@lyra:2]. A voluntary sample of current users cannot reveal whether students who walk or drive prefer the status quo, nor can it establish broader campus demand [@lyra:2]. These limitations suggest that the data describe existing users' preferences rather than overall access needs. This gap in representativeness reinforces why the boarding counts alone cannot resolve the question of whether the shuttle affects attendance, pointing instead toward the need for more inclusive measurement.

The evidence supports further investigation into usage patterns, not a causal link to academic presence. I want this paragraph to keep my uncertainty visible rather than sound more certain than the evidence allows.

live_draft_blocks.heading: Evidence
live_draft_blocks.content: The rider survey compounds this ambiguity by measuring only a subset of the population. Eighteen voluntary responses came from people already using the shuttle, and fourteen of them valued the later service [@lyra:2]. However, non-riders were not surveyed [@lyra:2]. A voluntary sample of current users cannot reveal whether students who walk or drive prefer the status quo, nor can it establish broader campus demand [@lyra:2]. These limitations suggest that the data describe existing users' preferences rather than overall access needs. This gap in representativeness reinforces why the boarding counts alone cannot resolve the question of whether the shuttle affects attendance, pointing instead toward the need for more inclusive measurement.

live_draft_blocks.heading: Recommendation
live_draft_blocks.content: I recommend extending the pilot for one term to capture the missing data. This extension is conditional: it buys time to answer the question the current evidence leaves open. Since non-riders were not surveyed in the initial data collection [@lyra:2], the committee cannot yet judge whether the service meets wider campus needs. The boarding figures alone do not resolve this gap. A one-term extension allows the collection of responses from non-riders, which is necessary to determine if demand exists beyond the current user base. This approach treats the current period as a measurement opportunity rather than a final endorsement of the service. It aligns with the need to move beyond the limitations of the voluntary rider sample.

live_draft_blocks.content: During this extension, I propose collecting brief survey responses from students who do not currently ride the shuttle. This step addresses the gap where no data on non-rider demand or barriers to access exist. The initial survey only described voluntary riders, so it cannot establish demand across all students [@lyra:2]. We must identify what prevents others from using the service before drawing conclusions about its broader impact. I also recommend against assessing cost or emissions during this term, as no such measurements were collected previously [@lyra:2]. Without baseline figures, any new assessment would lack context. This focused approach keeps the project manageable while gathering the specific access data needed to evaluate whether the shuttle serves a wider audience.
